newsitem.title: USA: Leaks, fire lead U.S. to review Mir station safety.
newsitem.headline: Leaks, fire lead U.S. to review Mir station safety.

text.p: Russia's troubled space station Mir has developed leaks in its cooling system, knocking out a device used to maintain breathable air on board, but backup systems are running and the leaks will be repaired on the weekend, NASA officials said on Friday.
The U.S. space agency will nevertheless review safety on Mir before sending any more astronauts to live and work there, a senior NASA official said.
Mir's current U.S. resident, Jerry Linenger, who has spent 82 days aboard the station, was to be replaced in mid-May by astronaut Michael Foale.
NASA's shuttle-Mir programme director Frank Culbertson said the space station was showing signs of its age but he was confident the Russians would keep it operating.
"They are dealing with more problems simultaneously then they have ever dealt with in the past," he said. "But I wouldn't say the station is falling apart."

"We are beefing up our flight readiness review process to be sure that leaving him (Foale) there is the right thing to do ... Right now it looks very positive. Unless there were some other failures, there is almost no likelihood we would change our plans," he said.

Culbertson's comments came after three separate cooling systems on Mir sprung leaks, causing the station to overheat and knocking out a device used to scrub carbon dioxide from the air. A backup chemical system, which can maintain a breathable atmosphere for eight days, was pressed into service on Thursday.
The cosmonauts were expected to plug the leak in one of the cooling systems on Saturday so they can reactivate the primary carbon dioxide scrubbing device, Culbertson said.

The cooling problem is the latest in a string of mishaps and breakdowns to hit the 11-year-old space station, including a brief but intense fire, the failure of the main oxygen generator and a stabilisation problem which put the station in a slow tumble.

An unmanned Progress resupply ship is due to blast off on Sunday and arrive at Mir two days later, carrying a repair kit for the oxygen generator, fresh oxygen generating chemicals and gear to further patch up the leaky cooling systems.
NASA officials were also scrambling to get a new Russian-made oxygen generator aboard the shuttle Atlantis, which is bound for Mir on May 15.
